turns.summary: New question: does a chatbot that mixes Malay and English (like we actually text) make young Malaysians trust it more and open up more?
turns.text:
QUESTION: Does a chatbot that code-switches between Malay and English, the way many Malaysian young adults actually text, increase perceived warmth, trust and depth of self-disclosure compared with a chatbot that uses standard English only?

WHY: Most human-AI disclosure research uses English-only agents and Western samples. In multilingual societies, language choice signals who is "one of us", so code-switching may be a powerful and under-studied social cue. That has direct design implications for local well-being apps.

INSTRUCTIONS:
- Frame code-switching as a social-identity and anthropomorphic cue, grounded in communication accommodation and in-group signalling ideas (describe prior work generally, no invented citations).
- Use a controlled experiment where the chatbot's content is identical across conditions and only the language style changes.
- Measure perceived warmth, competence, trust, and self-disclosure depth. Code disclosure from what people actually write, not just self-report.
- Check that the code-switched messages sound natural to native speakers before running the study.
- Flag risks: stereotyping, or the bot coming across as fake or mocking.

turns.summary: Drafted a 2-condition experiment: standard-English bot vs Malay–English code-switching bot, N=200, disclosure coded from real messages.
turns.text:
# Speaking Our Language: Code-Switching Chatbots and Self-Disclosure Among Malaysian Young Adults

## Background
People tend to open up more to partners who seem warm and similar to them. Prior work on human-AI interaction suggests that human-like cues in chatbots (names, empathy statements, casual tone) can raise perceived warmth and willingness to disclose. Almost all of this work uses English-only agents. In Malaysia, many young adults mix Malay and English in everyday messaging. Language mixing can signal shared identity and closeness, so a chatbot that code-switches might be read as an in-group member. This has not been tested.

## Research question and hypotheses
**RQ:** Does a Malay–English code-switching chatbot increase perceived warmth, trust and self-disclosure depth compared with a standard-English chatbot?
- **H1:** Participants rate the code-switching chatbot as warmer and more trustworthy.
- **H2:** Participants disclose more deeply to the code-switching chatbot.

## Method
**Design:** Online between-subjects experiment with two conditions: (A) standard English and (B) Malay–English code-switching. The chatbot follows the same scripted flow in both conditions. It asks about a recent stressful experience, reflects back, and asks follow-up questions.

**Participants:** 200 Malaysian adults aged 18–25 who report using both Malay and English, recruited through university mailing lists and social media.

**Procedure:** Participants chat with the bot for about 10 minutes, then complete questionnaires.

**Measures:**
- Perceived warmth and competence (adapted short rating items)
- Trust in the chatbot (adapted trust items)
- Self-disclosure depth: two coders rate each participant's messages for depth (from surface facts to personal feelings)
- Word count as a simple disclosure-quantity measure

**Analysis:** Independent-samples t-tests (or ANCOVA controlling for age and gender) comparing conditions on each outcome.

## Expected contribution
The first experimental test of code-switching as a social cue in chatbot conversations. It also gives practical guidance for designers of Malaysian mental-health and well-being chatbots.

## Limitations
- Scripted responses cannot adapt to what participants say, which lowers realism.
- Self-selected online sample.
- One 10-minute session cannot show longer-term effects.

turns.summary: REVISE. Big confound: code-switching is also more casual. Add a casual-English condition, measure people's own language habits, and add safeguards.
turns.text:
VERDICT: REVISE

STRENGTHS:
- A genuinely new question. Language style as a social cue in multilingual settings is almost untouched in human-AI disclosure research.
- Holding script content constant across conditions is the right move.
- Coding disclosure from participants' actual messages is stronger than relying on self-report alone.

PROBLEMS:
1. Main confound: code-switched Malay–English is also more casual than standard English. If condition B wins, we cannot tell whether code-switching or informality caused it. A casual-English condition is needed.
2. Who code-switches differs. Malaysia is linguistically diverse, and Malay–English mixing is not equally natural for every young adult (it depends on home language, ethnicity and region). The participants' own code-switching habits and language dominance are not measured, so the cue may feel "in-group" to some and odd to others.
3. Authenticity risk. Badly written code-switching can feel fake, try-hard or even mocking. The draft drops the naturalness check that the instructions asked for.
4. Mechanism missing. The theory says code-switching works through perceived similarity or in-group belonging, but nothing measures that, so we cannot test why it works.
5. Ethics. Asking about a recent stressful experience can surface distress. There is no screening, stop option, local support information or debrief.
6. Sample size is not justified. There is no power analysis, and adding a third condition changes the required N.
7. Coding is under-specified: no coding scheme, no inter-rater reliability target.

REQUIRED FIXES:
1. Add a casual-English condition (three conditions: formal English, casual English, Malay–English code-switching).
2. Measure each participant's code-switching frequency, language dominance and home language; test them as moderators.
3. Pilot the scripts with native-speaker ratings of naturalness and only use scripts that pass a set threshold.
4. Add perceived similarity / in-group belonging as a mediator.
5. Add safeguarding: exclude people in current crisis, allow stopping at any time, show local support contacts, debrief.
6. Run an a priori power analysis for three groups.
7. Define the disclosure-depth coding levels and require acceptable inter-rater reliability (for example, kappa ≥ .70).

turns.summary: Revised: 3 conditions (formal, casual, code-switched), N≈250 from a power analysis, naturalness pilot, in-group similarity as the mechanism.
turns.text:
CHANGES:
- Added a casual-English condition to separate code-switching from informality (now 3 conditions).
- Added participant language background as a moderator and perceived in-group similarity as a mediator.
- Added a native-speaker naturalness pilot, a power analysis, a defined coding scheme and a safeguarding protocol.

# Speaking Our Language: Malay–English Code-Switching as a Social Cue in Chatbot Self-Disclosure (Revised Brief)

## Question
Does a chatbot that code-switches between Malay and English increase perceived warmth, trust and self-disclosure depth among Malaysian young adults, beyond the effect of simply sounding casual?

## Hypotheses
- **H1:** Warmth and trust will be highest for code-switching, then casual English, then formal English.
- **H2:** Disclosure depth will be higher for code-switching than casual English. This is the key test that separates code-switching from informality.
- **H3:** The effect of code-switching is mediated by perceived in-group similarity.
- **H4:** The effect is stronger for participants who code-switch often in daily life.

## Method
**Design:** Online between-subjects experiment with three conditions: formal English, casual English, and Malay–English code-switching. All three use the same scripted conversation flow. Only the language style changes.

**Script pilot:** 20 native Malay–English bilinguals rate each script for naturalness and appropriateness. A script is used only if it reaches a preset mean rating (for example, ≥ 4 on a 5-point scale). Any line rated as awkward or mocking is rewritten.

**Participants:** About 250 Malaysian adults aged 18–25. A power analysis for a three-group comparison with a small-to-medium effect (f = 0.20, α = .05, power = .80) gives roughly 250. Recruitment is stratified so that participants' home language groups are represented.

**Measures:**
- Perceived warmth, competence and trust (short adapted rating scales)
- Perceived in-group similarity ("This chatbot talks like people I know")
- Self-disclosure depth, coded into three levels (facts, thoughts and opinions, feelings and vulnerabilities) by two blind coders, with kappa ≥ .70 required
- Participant's own code-switching frequency, language dominance and home language

**Analysis:** One-way ANCOVA across the three conditions with planned contrasts (code-switching vs casual English for H2). A mediation model for H3 and moderated regression for H4.

**Safeguarding:** Exclude people who report being in current crisis. Participants can stop at any time. Malaysian support contacts are shown before and after the chat. Full debrief about the language manipulation.

## Contribution
Separates a cultural-linguistic cue from general informality, and tests why it works (in-group similarity) and for whom (frequent code-switchers). It gives evidence-based guidance on whether local well-being chatbots should "speak like us".

## Limitations
Scripted responses limit realism. The results apply to Malay–English mixing among young adults and may not transfer to other language pairs. It is a single-session study.

turns.summary: ACCEPT: “Speaking Our Language”. Lesson: when a cue comes bundled with another (here, informality), separate them from the start.
turns.text:
DECISION: ACCEPT
TITLE: Speaking Our Language: Malay–English Code-Switching as a Social Cue in Chatbot Self-Disclosure
SUMMARY: This study tests whether a chatbot that mixes Malay and English like Malaysian young adults do makes people feel closer to it and open up more. A casual-English control condition makes sure any effect comes from the language mixing itself, not just from sounding informal.
LESSON: When a cue comes bundled with other features (here, code-switching with informality), design a control that separates them from the start.

turns.summary: Opportunity scan → next: a validated bilingual chatbot script set (demand 4, supply 1). Almost nobody shares these.
turns.text:
OPTION: Validated bilingual chatbot stimulus set (formal, casual and code-switched scripts) | 4 | 1 | Researchers in Southeast Asia need ready-made, naturalness-rated chatbot scripts; almost none are publicly available, and every study rebuilds them.
OPTION: Practitioner design guide for culturally adapted well-being chatbots in Malaysia | 4 | 2 | App teams want concrete language and tone guidance, but most existing guides are Western and English-only.
OPTION: Policy brief on AI companions and youth well-being in Malaysia | 4 | 2 | Policy interest is rising, but local evidence summaries are scarce.
OPTION: Narrative review of anthropomorphic cues in chatbots | 3 | 4 | Useful, but several reviews of anthropomorphism already exist.
CHOICE: Validated bilingual chatbot stimulus set (formal, casual and code-switched scripts)

Note: these demand and supply scores are my own estimates from general knowledge, not market data.
